In full, it should read: "Those who receive, uphold, recite, and properly study the Buddha's precepts," and so forth.
As for "king" (guó), a small one is called a "state" (bāng) and a large one is called a "kingdom" (guó).
The three yang lines arranged side by side resemble the Way of Qian, forming the number three.
Within the single qi, this expresses how the sage attains the One.
Thus, the *I Ching* says:
"The king and sovereign attain the One to govern the world."
One is the agent and three are the objects;
these so-called "Three Powers" (sancái) are heaven, earth, and humanity.
To unify the one through the three is what is meant by "King."
Because he is born of the king, he is called a prince.
As for "the hundred officials," this is a collective enumeration of all the various offices; thus it is said "hundred," as in the expression "the hundred surnames" (the common people).
It is not merely a matter of one hundred men.
A Chancellor (Xiang-zai) assists the King in deliberating the Way and coordinates state affairs, harmonizing the principles of Yin and Yang.
Because he is the chief minister (zhu-xiang), he is called a Chancellor.
"Bhikṣu" is here translated as "diligent male servant";
"bhikṣuṇī" is here translated as "diligent female servant.
[This refers to] entering from the small [vehicle] into the great.
The two assemblies both require [this];
since the formless realm lacks a body, only the desire and form realms are listed.
Those who do not belong to the preceding or succeeding categories are collectively termed "commoners" (shumin).
The "people" (min) are human beings.
Those born with the fivefold equality [of faculties] who serve as gatekeepers for the royal household are called *huanmen* (eunuchs).
Both men and women in the desire realm possess lustful desire.
This enumeration includes the maximum number of cases, extending even to the prostitution of men and women.
In ancient times, those who were punished for crimes and whose bodies were made subject to others for menial service were called "slaves" (nubi).
The eight classes are: first, the devas; second, the nāgas; third, the yakṣas; fourth, the gandharvas; fifth, the asuras; sixth, the garuḍas; seventh, the kiṃnaras; and eighth, the mahoragas.
The Mahoragas have horns upon their heads, while the rest of their bodies are like those of humans.
Among the non-human paths of the realm of ghosts, those who possess superior transformative powers are called *devas* (spirits);
those of middling and inferior classes are called *pretas* (ghosts).
Among the class of benevolent deities, those such as Vajrapāṇi are called Vajra-devas;
although they are great empowered bodhisattvas appearing in these forms, they must also truly receive the three sets of pure precepts.
Devas, nāgas, and others who manifest their bodies as humans to receive the bodhisattva precepts are called "transformed persons.
Animals of sharp faculties who understand human speech may also receive the precepts.
Since miscellaneous categories are still numerous, those listed above are merely a brief enumeration; hence the phrase "and so forth.
Because the precepts serve as the cause for subduing and severing [defilements], they are called "the foremost purity. This concludes the introductory text.
The Buddha’s discourse below, the second [section], the "Correct Exposition," is divided into two parts:
first, the elucidation of the ten grave offenses; second, the elucidation of the forty-eight minor precepts.
The first part is further divided into three sections.
First, the number is stated to encourage upholding;
second, there is the detailed explanation;
third, the conclusion encourages [practice].
The initial section also has four parts.
First, the enumeration of the number;
second, from "If one receives" onwards, the exhortation to recite the text.
First, it clarifies that failing to recite [the scriptures] causes harm and deficiency to one’s compassionate and vast vows, such that one is not a bodhisattva.
When body and speech depart from the texts and the conscious mind becomes coarse and wild,
the contemplation and cultivation of Buddha-nature will result in a deviation from awakening.
"Because one takes the six realms as one's object of concern, it is said that such a person is not a seed of Buddhahood.
"I am also like this," and so forth, cites the fruit to encourage the cause.
From "Third, all... onwards, it cites examples to encourage study.

Having briefly concluded the preceding three or four sections with a summary and an exhortation to uphold them, the second part provides a detailed explanation of the ten grave precepts in ten sections.
Regarding the first, the precept against taking human life: among the myriad practices of a bodhisattva, compassion is the foundation.
One regards sentient beings as one's own parents.
Yet, as they revolve through the six realms of existence, they do not recognize one another.
Therefore, the subsequent text says:
To kill and eat them is to kill my own parents;
it is an extreme violation of compassion.
For this reason, I have first established this precept.
What is called "killing" is the severing of life.
From the initial descent of consciousness until old age and death, the severing of that life which maintains the continuity of the stream is collectively termed killing.
There are two conditions for this universal application:
first, having received the bodhisattva vows;
second, abiding in one's natural state without being deranged or otherwise impaired.
Because this applies to all precepts, it is called "universal object" (sāmānyālambana).
It will not be mentioned again below.
The "specific object" (viśeṣālambana) possesses four [characteristics].
First, there must be a human being; second, the perception that it is a human being; third, the intent to kill; and fourth, the severing of life—only then is an offense committed.
If these conditions are lacking, a light offense is incurred.
Within each individual precept, these three factors are fully present.
First, the prohibition of evil;
second, the injunction to practice good;
third, the enumeration of faults and the formulation of offenses.
The first section also has three parts.
First, it identifies the person and enumerates the acts of killing.
Second, following the causes, it establishes the formation of the karmic action of killing.
Third, the phrase "even down to" uses a light case to illustrate a heavy one.
The initial expression "if a son of the Buddha" is a general term referring to those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta and received the bodhisattva precepts.
Those born from the Buddha-dharma are collectively termed "sons of the Buddha.
Regarding the act of killing oneself, there are five distinct phrases;
of these, the first two concern self-killing.
First, killing one's own body; second, killing the bodies of others.
Regarding the killing of one's own body, there are three meanings.
First, taking one's own life with an evil mind.
Second, to take one's own life out of loathing for the body violates the holy teachings in both cases and incurs a light defilement.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
It is said that while the body is impermanent, one does not speak of wearying of or detaching from the body.
Third, for the sake of bringing forth [beings] and establishing the Path, one sacrifices the body to save sentient beings,
as in the case of Prince Sattva and others.
Therefore, the subsequent text states that if one causes others to relinquish their own lives and so forth, one gains merit and incurs no offense.
Second, regarding the full commission of a *pārājika* offense through killing another by oneself:
next is the case of instructing another to kill.
If one instructs another to kill, and that person dies before the instruction was even given, one still commits a grave offense. Why?

Because the precept is inexhaustible; it differs from the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna which state that the precept is lost at the end of life, and thus [in our tradition] one incurs the *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) through the preparation (*prayoga*).
Third, praising the killer through three types of skillful means.
This refers to praising the virtues of another when seeing them in the act of killing.
First, praising the person capable of killing.
Second, praising the method of killing:
as stated in the Vinaya, using such phrases as "this is a way to live well" constitutes praising killing through skillful means.
Fourth, rejoicing in the act: this refers to rejoicing after the killing has already been committed.
Because one rejoices in whatever is seen or heard. Fifth,
even down to those who kill by means of incantations, the signs of killing are still manifold,
including such categories as blades, staves, pits, traps, poisons, and the like.
Because instances of killing through incantations are rare, [the text] bypasses many categories and states "up to and including" (*yāvat*),
such as cursing a person to bring about the end of their life.
Next, it enumerates the four distinct permutations regarding the completion of the karmic action of killing.
Taking the intent to kill as the cause,
with weapons such as swords and staves as the conditions,
one employs the preparatory means as the method.
Making killing one's primary occupation constitutes a karmic transgression.
Since three instances of light offenses are cited as a way to illustrate even heavier ones, it is said "even down to those with life.
Thus, one should know that apart from humans, all such acts constitute minor defilements.
Although there is no separate rule for this in the text below, it should be inferred by logical extension.
For example, the prohibition against setting fires in the spring and summer is intended to protect living plants and trees,
as well as to prevent injury to the lives of sentient beings.
However, the offense incurred is light.
Next, this is the Bodhisattva’s lower precept enjoining the practice of goodness;
it states that "constantly abiding in a mind of compassion" refers to unconditioned (anālambana) compassion.
It accords with principle;
because its essence is identical to the *dharmadhātu* and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is called "permanently abiding.
Thirdly, conversely, the text below cites the transgression to conclude the offense.
What is called *pārājika* is here translated as "defeat by another" (*tashengchu*).
To maintain the precepts in accordance with principle so as to realize the fruit of sainthood is termed "the work of a Buddha";
this is precisely the state of self-victory.
Violating the prohibitions and falling into hell is called a demonic deed (*mārakarman*).
This corresponds to the second *pārājika* offense, the precept against taking what is not given.
It is because of this that unjust seizure leads to the loss of life and the destruction of the path; there is nothing that does not stem from this cause.
This one rule was established next because even virtuous people could not yet avoid it.
It is distinguished by four conditions:
first, stealing an object belonging to another worth five *māṣakas* or more.
If one steals their own property, it does not constitute a grave offense.
Second, there must be the perception that the object has an owner.
Third, there must be the intention to steal.
Fourth, one commits an offense immediately upon lifting [the object] from its original place;
if the requisite conditions are lacking, the offense is minor.
Regarding the text, there are also three parts.
First, the initial formulation of the precepts prohibits evil;
second, the Bodhisattva section below prescribes the performance of good;
third, the subsequent sections below enumerate transgressions and define the offenses.
The initial text is divided into three parts.
First, the titles are listed to introduce the subject of theft.
Second, the factors that constitute the karmic action of theft are enumerated.
Third, from "down to" (*yāvat*) the lowest, the light case is used to illustrate the heavy.
The initial text states that "stealing by oneself" refers to stealing property worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more from another person.
Regarding those who instruct others to steal: even if they do not personally profit from it, because the harm to the object is profound, the offense is classified as grave.
Regarding those who steal through expedient means—whether by way of entrustment or barter—exchanging the short for the long or the coarse for the fine:
if there is a mind of theft and the value exceeds five coins, it is all classified as a grave offense.
Taking objects by means of incantations is called "stealing through spells.
Regarding the subsequent text on the causes of stealing: one's own mind acts as the cause, while external assistance serves as the condition.
To exert effort in creating the conditions for theft is "stealing the Dharma.
Constantly contemplating acts of theft as one's primary task is called "the karma of stealing.
The third point uses a minor case to illustrate a major one.
If one acts as a master over spirits and ghosts,
does not cast the tally (of one's own faults), and has not yet severed the intent to beg for the property of bandits—
then even a single needle, a blade of grass, or anything valued at five *qián* or less constitutes a minor offense (*āpatti*).
Therefore, this is raised as an analogy.
Next, regarding the injunction to practice goodness:
"The Buddha-nature" refers to relying on the principle of the Buddha-nature and acceding to the Buddha's teachings and Dharma.
Taking compassion of the same essence as its foundation,
it assists in the cultivation of sympathetic joy.
Because it causes all people to give rise to the merit and the bliss of wisdom of the five perfections, it is said that "one should generate [joy]," and so forth.
The third section, regarding the enumeration of faults and the formalization of the offense,
is as stated in the text. As for the third precept, the precept against engaging in unchaste conduct,
the *Mahā-śāstra* states:
Although sexual desire does not afflict other sentient beings, it binds the mind;
through private passions and dissolute indulgence, one revolves in the cycle of cause and effect.
Drifting and drowning in the river of craving, one transmigrates through the five destinies—all of which arise from this.
Therefore, the gravity of the offense is next established.
Specifically, four conditions must be present:
first, there must be sentient beings who are male and female.
Second, there is the lustful mind;
third, the employment of means;
fourth, the conjunction with the object, at which point the offense is committed.
Regarding the offenses committed through the lack of conditions, there are also three according to the text:
first, designating the names and establishing prohibitions to cease evil;
second, establishing regulations to practice goodness.
This consists of three parts, which in turn reverse [the previous] and cite the transgression to conclude the offense.
The first part also has three sections;
the first clarifies the matter of the offense committed.
Next, the accomplishment of karma is explained.
From "three" down to "inferior," human beings, women, and so forth are cited as examples.
Regarding the first point, "self-indulgence in lust": (1) if one indulges in lust with oneself, such as with a soft-spined being, it constitutes a grave offense;
(2) if one indulges in lust with another when all the necessary conditions are met, it constitutes a grave offense.
As for instructing others to indulge in lust, because the pleasure does not reach one's own body, one incurs only a light defilement, which is the same as for the Śrāvakas.
Regarding "all women and so forth," this excludes those who are insane or deluded.
As for the subsequent phrase "due to causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*), the defiled mind’s discursive thought constitutes the cause,
while improper conceptualization and adornment constitute the condition.
Its nature consists of formal deportment as its dharma;
its function consists of tending toward the accomplishment of the aforementioned matters in every thought-moment.
Regarding the third [category], it refers to non-human females and so forth; as for the intermediate statement concerning "female spirits," it refers to female ghosts and deities.
If one, within one's own mind, requests that [the deity] manifest its form to engage in unchaste conduct—
specifically with two men or two women, which is termed "non-path"—
one incurs a grave offense in each case.
All other remaining outflows and such are collectively categorized as minor offenses.
Next, the Bodhisattva’s lower precepts enjoin the practice of goodness.
Regarding what is called "pure dharma," it refers to the cultivation of the contemplation of Buddha-nature, whose essence is free from the three delusions.
Because it involves both practicing for oneself and transforming others, it is said that "pure dharmas are bestowed upon others.
Third, regarding the section on citing faults and concluding the offense, the term "six relatives" refers to the kinship of six persons.
First, the relatives of the father refer to paternal grandparents, paternal aunts, uncles, and so forth.
Second, the relatives of one's mother, namely maternal aunts and so forth;
third, one's own relatives, namely parents, brothers, and one's wife and children from that time;
fourth, the relatives of one's wife, namely her sisters and so forth.
Fifth, relatives by marriage on the side of sons and daughters refers to those such as new brides;
sixth, relatives by marriage on the side of brothers refers to those such as sisters-in-law.
Regarding these, there are two meanings.

When a single defiled mind arises toward a certain object, it simultaneously gives rise to the defiled minds of all other people without discriminating between the six types of kin; therefore, it is said that they "arise in reverse.
Here, "arise" (qi) means "to be produced" (sheng).

Second, because one personally engages in non-celibacy toward all objects—without discrimination, including animals and the six classes of relatives—as a cause for inciting evil in others, it is said that "one conversely incites all [evil], etc."
This refers to the "defiled dharma" (hīna-dharma) which, when given to others, causes them to give rise to defilement;

it is contrary to the aforementioned "pure dharma" (viśuddha-dharma) which, when given to others, causes them to sever evil. Therefore, it is said that it "instead leads to the opposite," thus concluding the refutation of the fault.
The fourth precept against great falsehood:
to claim what one has not attained as having been attained, thereby deceiving the noble ones and misleading the common people;
because this deludes and agitates the world and improperly invites fame and profit, it constitutes a grave offense.
It possesses five distinct conditions:
first, there must be a sentient being;
second, there must be the perception of that being as a sentient being.
Third, conceiving a deceptive mind;
fourth, claiming superhuman attainments;
fifth, the offense is incurred as soon as the other person understands.
The conditions for the offense are minor.
According to the text, there are three parts:
first, the designation of the name and the establishment of the rule to prohibit evil.
Next, he establishes the practice of performing wholesome deeds.
Third, he enumerates the faults and defines the transgressions.
The first section also consists of three parts.
First, the transgression is explained;
second, the formation of karma is explained;
third, the light case is cited to illustrate the heavy.
Regarding the initial statement on "lying to oneself":

if one claims to have attained the four fruits, the eight stages of persons, the stage of seeing the truths (*darśana-bhūmi*), and so forth up to the purification of the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*), or from the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) upward through the higher stages, such a claim constitutes a grave offense.
If one claims to have attained the five objects of mindfulness, the stages of Heat, Peak, Patience, and the Supreme Worldly Dharma, or the various skillful means of the stage of Dry Wisdom—
since these are all dharmas of ordinary beings— one merely incurs a minor offense.

Regarding the second case, "teaching others": if one teaches others to speak of having attained the dharmas of the noble ones (ārya), claiming that the merit belongs to them, one commits only a minor offense (light defilement).
However, if one teaches others and they have already [spoken of] themselves as noble ones, one commits a grave offense.
"Deceptive speech through skillful means" refers to falsely presenting a different matter to cause another to give rise to the understanding that one is a sage.
It is called "skillful means" (*upāya*) because, for example, one says, "Today I did not enter the first stage of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)," and so forth. Thus it is termed "means."
Next, within the text: giving rise to a deceitful mind internally serves as the cause;
externally aspiring for fame and profit serves as the condition;
and skillfully devising expedient means serves as the method.
To constantly harbor this intent as one's habitual practice constitutes the third [type].
Furthermore, from the minor to the grave—using the light to illustrate the heavy—it includes even minor false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).

For example, if one says, "Who has attained the contemplation of impurity? and then gives rise to such a claim within a gathering, it constitutes a false speech regarding name and body (*nāmakāya-mṛṣāvāda*).
To lie about one's name or identity when questioned in secret is called verbal falsehood;
to fail to respond when questioned openly is called mental falsehood.
Failing to declare that one has attained the state of an Arya constitutes a minor offense of defilement (duṣkṛta).

Next, regarding the injunction to practice virtue, the terms "right speech" and "right view" refer to knowing through the mind of the Middle Way according to reality, according to things as they are, and according to their conceptualization; this is called "viewing.
Because one practices this oneself and exhorts others to do so, it is said that "one constantly gives rise to [it], and others likewise give rise to it," and so forth.
Third, the formal accusation of the offense:
this is not merely termed "deviant intercourse," but refers to false speech in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions;
here, because it constitutes a major falsehood and a major deviance, the offense is formally established.
The fifth precept concerns the selling of intoxicants.
"Selling" (酤) is a term for commercial trade;
"intoxicant" (酒) refers to a drug that causes stupor and intoxication.
There are thirty-six faults of alcohol;
because it is a gateway to heedlessness, it is strictly prohibited.
It possesses four distinct conditions.
First, actual alcohol; second, the perception that it is actual alcohol;
third, the intention to sell it.
Fourth, if one bestows [the object] upon another person, one commits an offense immediately;
if the requisite conditions are lacking, the offense is minor.
According to the text, there are also three [points].
First, the names are designated to establish prohibitions that stop evil;
second, the prohibitions are established to command the practice of good;
third, faults are cited to conclude the offenses.
The initial section also has three parts:
first, clarifying the transgression;
second, clarifying the formation of karma.
Third, the light case is raised to illustrate the heavy.
First, it is understandable that one who sells [liquor] oneself commits an offense;
as for instructing another, if one instructs another to sell on one's own behalf, one commits a grave offense.
Teaching others to sell their own goods constitutes a minor offense.
Regarding the subsequent formation of karma,
it has as its cause personally engaging in the production of rice, flour, and so forth.
The external requisites such as clothing and so forth serve as conditions;
the skillful means of harmonious adjustment is called "Dharma" (the teaching);
and constant practice is the activity, which is called "Karma" (action).
Third, regarding all cases below, this is an instance of "lifting the light to illustrate the heavy":
grain, medicinal herbs, grasses, and trees combined to form something that is not genuine flour or rice, but merely resembles wine;
selling such a substance incurs a minor offense.
If one cannot even sell imitation wine, how much less true wine?
Next, the Bodhisattva issues a decree below to cause the practice of goodness;
this refers to the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) for those who are clear-sighted and wise.
The third [section] concludes by returning to the lower [level], where the transgressions are raised and the offenses established; this may be understood.
The sixth [section] explains the names and virtues of the fourfold assembly and the precepts regarding their transgressions.
A bodhisattva, in the vast protection of his heart, conceals evil and extols the good for the sake of the Triple Gem.
How could one permit the disparagement of the Dharma or the defilement of the faithful mind?
Because such acts deviate from the practice of benefiting others, they are established as grave offenses (*pārājika*).
Specifically, these require seven conditions to be fulfilled.
First, speaking of a bodhisattva among the fourfold assembly of śrāvakas as being superior in name and virtue;
second, forming the perception of them as such;
third, with a malicious mind, intending to speak of their faults.
Fourth, it is directed toward outsiders;
fifth, one perceives them as outsiders;
sixth, the phrasing of the words is clear and distinct.
Seventh, the offense is committed as soon as the person before one understands;
if the conditions are incomplete, the offense is minor.
Regarding the text, there are also three [sections].
First, the names are stated to establish the prohibitions that restrain evil.
Second, from "Furthermore, a bodhisattva... onwards, the prohibitions are established to enjoin the performance of good.
Third, from "Furthermore, a bodhisattva... onwards, faults are cited to conclude the offenses.
The first section also has two parts:
first, clarifying the transgression;
second, clarifying the formation of karma.

The initial text states that both performing [the act] oneself and instructing others results in a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), as the nature of the damage to the object is identical. The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* says:
"Though the campaka flower may wither, it still surpasses all other flowers."
Bhikṣus who have broken the precepts are still superior to non-Buddhists;
thus, the *Adornment Sūtra* (*Ābharaṇa-sūtra*) states:
"One who commits transgressions is called a bodhisattva."
Those who commit no offenses are called non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
For this reason, even if they do commit transgressions, they must not be disparaged.
The subsequent passage states that the internal mind serves as the cause.
It takes those objects of transgression as its conditions,
establishes rules of conduct as its phenomena,
and has the purpose of instructing persons as its function.
Next, regarding the injunction to practice goodness, those referred to as "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika) include everyone outside the seven assemblies;
these non-Buddhists are indeed evil persons.
As for the "evil persons of the two vehicles," they are those who, weary of the truths of suffering and its origin, cultivate the path toward cessation.
To emerge alone from birth and death is called the Śrāvaka-yāna;
to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination either in reverse or in forward order with the intent of seeking liberation from suffering,
yet with a weak aspiration for the benefit of others, is called the Pratyekabuddha-yāna.
This mind, being itself evil, is called an "evil person.
One who does not believe in the Mahāyāna says it is neither the Dharma nor the Vinaya and will certainly fall into suffering.
Therefore, one causes the compassionate mind to speak of the Great [Vehicle] so that faith may arise.
This is because compassion is able to uproot suffering.
The three fetters are as stated in the text.
The seventh is the precept against praising oneself and disparaging others.
To praise one's own merits while disparaging the great virtues of others is an extreme form of harming sentient beings; therefore, it is established as a grave offense.
This is specifically characterized by five conditions.
First, the object of one who has received the precepts and possesses virtue is the same as the initial condition.
Second, forming the perception of that person.
Third, possessing both praise and disparagement.
Fourth, with an evil mind, one praises or slanders another person in their presence;
fifth, the offense is committed once the other person understands the meaning.
If these conditions are lacking, the offense is minor.
Regarding the text, there are also three parts:
first, designating names and establishing prohibitions to cease evil;
second, establishing regulations to practice good.
Third, the summary of the transgression and the establishment of the offense.
This section has two parts.
First, it clarifies that for the matter of the offense, whether one commits it oneself or instructs another to do so, both incur a grave offense.
Next, it is explained that for the completion of karma, internal greed and pride serve as the cause;
envying others' gains serves as the condition;
and skillfully devising expedient means serves as the method.
Making this one's primary concern constitutes a transgression of name and practice.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva must, at the very least, restrain himself and cause others to perform good deeds.
Thirdly, if one personally commits a violation through negligence, the details are as stated in the text.
Furthermore, out of stinginess, he adds to this by reviling the precepts.
Since for a Bodhisattva who gathers in sentient beings, giving is the foremost of the ten thousand practices,
how could he further be so base and parsimonious as to add insult to injury?
Therefore, the gravity of the offense is established by the separate presence of six conditions.
The first is that the object is of the highest degree.
Second, one possesses wealth and property;
third, one harbors two types of perceptions;
fourth, one extensively applies a malicious mind to disparage, insult, beat, and revile [the other].
Fifth, the person before one understands and accepts [the instruction].
Sixth, causing another to return empty-handed constitutes an offense;
if the necessary conditions are lacking, the offense is minor.
According to the text, there are three parts:
first, designating names and instituting prohibitions to cease evil;
second, instituting prohibitions to practice goodness.
Third, the formal accusation and the determination of the offense.
This section has two parts;
the first clarifies the matter of the offense.
Both practicing stinginess oneself and teaching others to do so constitute a grave offense only when the aforementioned conditions are fully met.
Next, regarding the formation of karma, stinginess serves as the cause,
while wealth and the Dharma serve as the conditions.
To conceal, guard, and seal [the Dharma] is their dharma;
they are devoted to the practice of stinginess and parsimony.
Subsequently, the Bodhisattva established lower precepts to compel them to perform virtuous deeds.
To be destitute of both wealth and the Dharma is to be poor in both respects.
Since my practice is not yet deep, how could I possibly relinquish everything?
If one gives according to one's heart and offers kind words of consolation and thanks, there is no transgression.
Third, the Bodhisattva cites an example of a transgression to conclude the discussion on offenses.

Regarding the phrase "verses and stanzas" (*gāthā*): "verses" (*pada*) refers to a small portion of that which expresses [the meaning], while "stanzas" (*gāthā*) refers to the complete sense within the teaching.
For example, from "The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body" up to "therefore I take refuge."
This praises the Buddha for being fully endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Regarding "a single atom of Dharma," this uses a single virtuous word as an illustration.
The ninth [precept] concerns the precept against harboring anger and refusing to accept an apology.
Now, as a bodhisattva, one should cherish patience;
yet to harbor malice and resentment within the mind instead harms compassion and damages the Way.
No thief of merit is greater than anger and hatred.
Because a minor resentment in this life may become a great enmity in the future, [the Buddha] established these grave offenses.
They require six specific conditions:
first, there must be an object that is either superior or middling.
Second, the perception directed toward the person who caused the offense;
third, the failure to cease the mind of anger;
fourth, the offender’s confession and apology.
Fifth, it is shown that one does not accept the perception [of the offense].
Sixth, the offense is committed as soon as the person before one understands;
if the necessary conditions are lacking, the offense is minor.
Regarding the text, there are also three parts:
first, designating the names and enacting prohibitions to cease evil;
second, enacting regulations to perform good.
Third, the summary of the offense and its transgression.
This section also has two parts.
First, it clarifies that the act of committing the offense—whether through one's own anger or by instructing others—is grave when all the requisite conditions are met.
Next, in explaining the formation of karma:
the internal mind serves as the cause,
while the external object serves as the condition.
The accumulation of the aggregates constitutes the ritual procedure for the Dharma;
that which takes aversion as its primary activity is called karma.
Subsequently, the Bodhisattva restrains those below [the laity] and commands them to practice virtue.
As stated in the text, there are three [cases].
Conversely, the following section cites the faults and concludes with the offense.
This extends even to non-sentient beings, which refers to harboring anger toward insentient things.
It is like a person who, out of a mind of anger, strikes at their livelihood— even hitting wood or stone— and yet gives rise to anger toward that which is not a sentient being;
this is cited as an illustration of a minor offense.
The phrase "by means of harsh speech, etc. correctly concludes the fault.
This is the tenth precept concerning the assistance of slandering the Triple Gem.
That which possesses rare and supreme virtues is called a "gem" (ratna).
It is called slander because it is an irrational defilement;
it specifically possesses six conditions.
First, one assists in the slander before an assembly.
Second, the Mahāyāna single essence and distinct-aspect Three Jewels;
third, giving rise to the two aforementioned conceptions;
fourth, possessing a mind of slander.
If one speaks five words clearly, it constitutes an offense;
if the person before one understands, it is an immediate offense (*pārājika*).
If the necessary conditions are lacking, the offense is minor.
Regarding the text, there are also three parts:
first, designating the name to cause one to cease evil;
second, causing one to practice good.
Third, regarding the section on "exceeding the limit by speaking," there are two parts in the initial text.
First, it clarifies the matter of the offense.
Both self-reproach and instructing others [in such reproach] constitute grave offenses.
Next, the formation of karma is explained;
this is the internal cause.
With wrong views and so forth as conditions,
one skillfully constructs provisional dharmas;
this mind, taking these dharmas as its task, is called karma.
Next, the Bodhisattva prescribes the practice of performing good deeds as a lower restraint.

Regarding those referred to in the middle [section] as "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika): this refers to those whose minds wander outside the perfect principle, including even the three schools that are external to the external, all of whom are termed non-Buddhists.
Because slandering the Buddha with even a single word should always be regarded with deep regret,
it is likened to a spear-point (*śalya*).
A spear is a weapon two *zhang* in length, used for mounting on war chariots.
The three offenses for transgressing the precepts are as stated in the text.
Regarding "well-trained" and below, the third section consists of three parts encouraging [the practice].
First, it presents the dharmas to be upheld.
Second, the exhortation;
third, the reference to the extensive [text]. Each of these three sections has two parts.
Regarding the first section, there are two parts: first, a general enumeration of the persons.
The phrase "well-trained" (suśikṣita) is a term of praise.
Next, from "this bodhisattva" onwards, the Dharma is presented;
because the fruit is spoken of within the context of the cause, it is called *mokṣa*.
*Vinaya* means liberation.
Next, one should provide both admonition and exhortation below;
first, the exhortation to study and uphold [the precepts].
Next, if there is a lapse, this passage points it out to reveal what constitutes upholding [the precepts].
The initial mention of "dust" (*rajas*) is as it is said in worldly parlance: "A subject has not rendered even a speck of dust's worth of service to the state.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is like protecting a life-preserving bag so that not even a speck of dust [of water] enters.
This cites the smallest case as an illustration.
Next, citing the loss of the middling [benefits], there are two parts.
First, it clarifies the ten benefits lost in the present.
Next, the retribution for the three miserable realms is explained.

Regarding the first passage: because one has violated one's original great vow and failed to maintain the Bodhicitta—the Dharma that is without regret or loss—the Bodhicitta cannot manifest before one;
therefore, it is said that one is unable to give rise to Bodhicitta in the present.
The minor kings and universal monarchs (cakravartin) lose their status because they take the precepts as their cause;
since the fruit perishes when the cause is lost, it is said that they "also lose" [their sovereignty] and so forth.
Likewise, monks, nuns, and others, having lost their precepts, will receive retribution by entering the three evil realms.
How could one possibly serve as a witness for another regarding their successive stages?
Therefore, it is said that they also lose their status as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and so forth.
The phrase "the ten stages of departure" (daśa-prasthāna) enumerates the loss of these successive stages.
The first four are causes.
The "wonderful fruit" of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature refers to the fruit of wondrous enlightenment.
The eternally abiding Buddha-nature extends throughout the beginning and the end.
Now, in contrast to the ultimate stage,
it is called the "wondrous fruit" because it is the fruit of the Buddha-nature’s eternal abiding;
this is also like how the *Renwang jing* does not clarify the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Next, it is explained that they fall into the three evil realms.

Because their violation of the prohibitions differs, their retribution leads them into the three evil realms; this refers to the varying degrees of diligence or negligence with which they hear the Dharma.
The kindness of parents in their compassionate upbringing is profound;
the protection of the Triple Gem is ultimate and can be relied upon as a refuge.
Since they have not heard the names [of these protectors], they have no ground for reliance; therefore, these alone are singled out for mention.
A kalpa refers to time.
Each of the four phases—formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness—consists of twenty periods of increase and decrease.
One such period of increase and decrease constitutes one minor kalpa.
Twenty periods of increase and decrease constitute one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
Eighty periods of increase and decrease constitute one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*), and so forth.
The phrase "by these [examples]" concludes the exhortation; the "threefold" refers to the three types of beings, while the "below" points to the detailed exposition.
Second, first there is the exhortation to study,
followed by the indication of the extensive version.
This extensive version of the sutra contains eighty thousand chapters on dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
In the *Tiantai Pusa jie shu* (Commentary on the Bodhisattva Precepts), the Tiantai śramaṇa Mingkuang revised and supplemented the text, subsequently clarifying the forty-eight minor precepts.
They are termed "minor" because they differ from the ten grave [precepts]; it is not that there is no transgression in violating them.
Because they accumulate, they are called "defilements" (*mala*).
Within this, there are three parts;
first, the connection between what precedes and what follows.
Next is the detailed explanation,
followed by the threefold summary;
the first is as stated in the text.
Next, the explanation is divided into five parts:
first, the initial thirty [verses] constitute three sections;
next, the following two groups of nine constitute two sections.
The first ten [verses] and the twelfth.
First, the explanation;
second, the concluding exhortation pointing toward the extensive [text].
The initial explanation is divided into ten parts.
First is the precept against disrespecting teachers and elders:
it is the principle of a bodhisattva that they should be humble and reverently support all sentient beings.
How much more so regarding teachers and elders— since the transgression of showing them disrespect and disobedience is extreme,
it is established at the head [of the precepts].
It is distinguished by four specific conditions.
First, it is a teacher;
second, one knows this;
third, one intentionally gives rise to contempt and arrogance.
Fourth, one commits an offense by failing to show respect with body and mind.
Regarding the text, there are three parts.
First, the title is stated and the recipient is exhorted to accept it.
Next, having already attained [the precepts],
the following section demonstrates the practice and instructs on their observance;
thirdly, the section beginning with "And the bodhisattva" concludes by defining the transgressions.
The "Kings of Initial Texts" are those who are among the minor kings scattered like grains of millet among men.
The "Wheel-turning Kings" are the noble kings of iron, copper, and so forth.
The Iron Wheel-turning King rules over one world-system.
A copper-wheel-turning king rules over two continents;
a silver-wheel-turning king, over three continents;
and a gold-wheel-turning king, over four continents.
If these high-ranking officials among the civil and military ministries do not receive the precepts, spirits and deities will not protect them;
how then can they govern the masses?
Therefore, it is urged that they should first receive [the precepts], and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas rejoice," it means that in accordance with the discipline (*vinaya*) of the Buddhas, all should indeed rejoice.
Next, regarding the phrase "the Elder (*sthavira*) and others":
among the Sangha, the foremost leader who is skilled in guiding the great assembly also carries the sense of a teacher.
The terms *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* are explained briefly as before.
A senior fellow student is called a "great fellow student" (*mahā-sabrahmacārin*).
Those who share the same right view are called "those of the same view" (*samadṛṣṭi*).
Those who practice the same path should be called "fellow practitioners.

However, when a bodhisattva descends into cessation and forms a bond that constitutes an offense, the terms such as "arrogant mind" (*māna*) are used: to exalt oneself is arrogance (*mada*), while to look down upon others is pride (*māna*).
The second is called "delusion," which arises from arrogance due to one's filial piety.
The phrase "those who are equal to oneself" uses a heavy case to illustrate a light one;
one ought to sell one's own body to repay the grace of those who have recently brought one to completion.
How much more so if one gives rise to contempt;
therefore, an offense is established.
As for the seven treasures: first, gold; second, silver; third, lapis lazuli; fourth, crystal; fifth, red pearl; sixth, musaragalva; seventh, agate.
"All things" refers to everything that exists in general.
Were it otherwise, it would merely mean not being filial, respectful, or making offerings, and so forth.
This is the second precept: abstaining from drinking alcohol.
Alcohol is a drug that causes delusion;
because grave transgressions arise from it, it is established as a prohibited offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
It possesses four distinct conditions.
First, it must be genuine alcohol;
second, one must perceive it as genuine alcohol;
third, there must be no circumstance of serious illness.
The offense is committed as soon as the four [liquids] enter the mouth.
In the Vinaya, drinking by mistake is not permitted;
this text establishes a formal prohibition for that reason.
Regarding the text, there are two further parts.
First, the designation of the name, the citation of the fault, and the establishment of the injunction to cease evil.
Second, from "If intentionally... onwards, the supplementary injunction and the determination of the offense.
The initial mention of "wine vessels" refers to empty vessels used for holding wine.
If one commits an offense even with an empty vessel, how much more so when encouraging others to drink?
From the hells and the realms of rebirth, beings are born among various species, even down to earthworms.
Therefore, it is said that one has "no hands.
Since even instructing others to drink is improper, how much more so is drinking it oneself?
Consequently, both acts are defined as offenses.
The offenses incurred by violating [the preceding rules] may be understood.
Third is the precept against eating meat.
It is the principle of a Bodhisattva to disregard their own person in order to save sentient beings.
How could it be permissible to consume the bodily parts of sentient beings? Therefore, it is established as a transgression.
It requires three specific conditions:
first, there must be the flesh of a sentient being.
Second, the perception of it as meat arises;
third, upon entering the mouth, one commits the offense.
According to the text, there are two [parts].
First, the title is presented to clarify the fault and establish the prohibition to restrain evil.
Second, from "If one intentionally eats... onwards, the prohibition is set forth and the offense is defined.
Fourth is the precept against eating the five pungent roots.
The bodies and mouths of Bodhisattvas are fragrant and pure;
conversely, those who consume foul and impure things are shunned by the worthy and holy.
For this reason, the prohibitions and offenses were established.
There are four distinct conditions:
first, the five pungent plants;
second, the perception that they are the five pungent plants.
Third, there is no occasion of serious illness;
fourth, eating constitutes an offense.
Regarding the text, there are two parts.
First, the person is identified by name to establish the prohibition and stop evil.
Next, the section beginning with "If intentionally" defines the offense for violating the regulation.
Regarding the first part, the "one large garlic" refers to what is commonly called *hú* (onion/garlic) in secular parlance.
2. *Gēcōng* (革葱) refers to leeks (*jiǔ*) and garlic (*xiè*), etc.;
3. *Xiè* (薤) is simply a type of onion, etc.;
4. *Lán cōng* (兰葱), *lìng* (䔉), *yě lìng* (野䔉), etc.
Five: digging canals, *laotuo*, *tong*, and *jiji*.
Next, the formulation of the offense is as in the text.
Fifth: the precept against failing to instruct in repentance.

A bodhisattva, out of compassion for sentient beings, should expose their transgressions to others, causing them to reform their past ways and strive to maintain purity by first adhering to the Right Path.
By rescuing the common people below and upholding the holy Dharma above, they repay the Buddha’s kindness; this is of the greatest benefit.
Therefore, the regulations were established to ensure careful observance.
Specifically, five conditions are set forth.
The first is the objective sphere of the transgression of the precepts.
Second, knowing what has been transgressed;
third, having no other obstructing conditions, such as bad discipline (*duḥśīla*) and so forth;
fourth, forming the intention to conceal it.
The fifth [category], common ritual acts, constitutes an offense immediately upon commission.
This section consists of two parts:
first, the enumeration of the names and the establishment of the matters to be performed.
Next, the bodhisattva descends and establishes the formal confession of offenses.
The five precepts are: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to engage in sexual misconduct; fourth, not to speak falsely; and fifth, not to drink intoxicants.
Abstaining from meat for the rest of one's life constitutes the five names of the Five Precepts.

As for the Eight Precepts: first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in sexual misconduct; fourth, [the same as above]; fifth, not sitting or lying on high, wide, or large beds; sixth, not wearing flowers, perfumes, necklaces, or applying oil to the body; seventh, not playing music oneself nor intentionally going to watch or listen to it; eighth, abstaining from food after midday. These constitute the fundamental rules.
These eight precepts may be undertaken for either a short or long duration;
whether received in their entirety or in part, they are all valid.
If one adds the rules against handling money or precious objects and eating after midday, they constitute the ten precepts.
Those who violate the prohibitions commit the two hundred and fifty [offenses] and so forth.
The seven heinous crimes (*saptānantarya*) are explained below.

The eight unfavorable conditions (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*) are: first, hell; second, hungry ghosts; third, animals; fourth, the northern continent (Uttarakuru); fifth, long-lived devas; sixth, those with worldly wisdom and eloquence; seventh, those with impaired faculties; and eighth, the periods before and after a Buddha’s appearance.
These eight are the fruits.
Since the fruit is produced by the cause, one may see the transgressions committed through their causes and bring them to repentance.
What, then, are these causes?
That is to say: violating the precepts is the cause for falling into hell;
stinginess and greed are the causes for becoming a hungry ghost;
and a lack of shame is the cause for becoming an animal.
To seek long life among humans, one observes the three refuges and the five precepts; this is the cause for rebirth in Uttarakuru.
To seek celestial pleasures, one observes the eight precepts and so forth; this is the cause for rebirth in the Heaven of Longevity.

while right nature is the object of focus.

This very body of mine is now the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The ultimate tenet elucidated by the Mahāyāna culminates herein.
From cause to fruition, there is nothing that transcends the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Therefore, the text cites those who do not study in order to exhort them toward cultivation.
The subsequent passage likens the seven categories of the Dharma-gate of the Unconditioned Path (asaṃskṛta-mārga) to the seven treasures.
Beyond these, all that is not the perfect and true path is termed "false view."
Because one does not comprehend the provisional, one incurs an offense;

The four *siddhāntas* adapt to the times; when the primary and auxiliary practices are combined, and the heterodox and orthodox principles are unified, one does not transgress the boundaries.

A bodhisattva who raises livestock should act in accordance with proper ritual decorum, possessing inner benevolence and compassion while refraining from external harm;
yet now, on the contrary, you raise and create illegal items to sell to others.
The offense is established because it increases faults for oneself and others.
It specifically requires four conditions;
the first is that the object is not a legitimate item.
Second, relying on one's power;
third, having an evil mind;
fourth, intentionally keeping [the animals] and selling them constitutes an offense.
Regarding the text, there are two parts.
First, the titles are listed to indicate improper matters.
Second, from "If intentionally... onwards, it describes the violation of the regulations and the resulting offense.
Initially, there are six [offenses]:
first, selling implements for killing;
second, keeping light scales and small measures.
Third, seizing wealth by exploiting the power of others;
fourth, binding humans and livestock with a harmful mind;
fifth, destroying successful undertakings.
The six items include cats and dogs.
Because these six things can all cause harm, their possession and use are prohibited.
As for wealth and property that come into one's hands, they fall under the preceding precept against stealing.
Now, because it is improper, a light offense is established. The establishment of the transgression is as stated in the text.
This is the thirty-third precept concerning the offense of wrong-doing for listening to [improper] views.
It is the proper principle for a bodhisattva to contemplate in a quiet place and uphold the sacred scriptures;
now, conversely, to observe and listen to what is not the Dharma, to engage in misconduct, to act contrary to the Dharma, and to incur public reproach—therefore, this is established as an offense.
There are three distinct conditions:
first, there must be an object present;
second, there must be the act of looking or listening with a malicious mind.
There are three instances where one commits an offense upon seeing or hearing. According to the text, there are three parts.
First, it identifies the mind that commits the offense.
Second, "observing all [transgressions]" below refers to raising up faults and preventing them through prohibitions.
Third, "if intentionally" below refers to the formal conclusion of an offense for violating the regulations.
Regarding the first point, "evil mind" (*akuśala-citta*) refers to a state of mind that does not seek reconciliation, but instead rejoices in ignorance; this is termed an "evil mind."
The subsequent text contains much meaning.
First, regarding the observation of those who fight: "fighting" refers to both physical combat and verbal quarreling.
This includes military arrays, soldiers, and generals—namely the armies of kings—as well as bandits and the like.
"Combat" refers to the armies of thieves and the like.
Whether one watches it oneself, instructs others to watch, attempts it, or treats it as a game, one must not view it; hence the word "etc.
Furthermore, one must not remain below to listen to music.
If others provide offerings for the purpose of providing entertainment and spectators, one may accept them without defilement and without committing an offense;
however, one must not engage in vulgar performances or mixed amusements.
The gambling games of *chupapu* (four-count) and *weiqi* (go) should be understood accordingly.
The game of *bala-se* (elephant chess) is a military game of the Western regions.
Each of the two players employs twenty jade elephants.
In this region as well, there is a version using a painted board as the playing field.
In the game of *ya*, one wins by capturing the opponent's pieces and seizing the main thoroughfare.
In *tanqi* (stone-skipping), one wins by using the fingers to launch the stone pieces so that they land at a greater distance.
*Liubo* (six-sided dice) is simply the game of double-sixes.
"Patting the ball" (*pāqiú*)—*qiú* means to kick; it refers to the manner of leaping and kicking.

It is also called "ball-patting" (*pāqiú*), which has the same meaning. "Throwing stones" (*zhìshí*)—it is also said that "throwing stones" (*zhìshí*) means to cast down (*tuò*). *Tuò* is pronounced with the *huó* rhyme.
In the game of *touhu* (pitch-pot), one throws coins, sticks, and other objects into a hole; each successful entry counts as a tally (*chou*).
Regarding the "pulling the path," it is sometimes called "encircling the straight.
Two people face each other, each with twelve pieces.
If one proceeds directly [toward the goal], one will fail; therefore, it is called the "Leading Path" (*kaidō*).
When the practice of the Eightfold Path is perfected, the eight paths interlace like a city wall.
As for the "mirror of the claws" and so forth, these are methods for ceasing heterodox practices.
The sorcerers of the Western Regions apply medicinal substances to their fingernails to manifest signs of good or ill fortune.
As for the *zhicao* (mushroom grass) and so forth—these three matters are known to indicate good or ill fortune through the recitation of mantras.
As for the skull, in foreign lands to the west, non-Buddhist practitioners strike the skulls of people to discern the causes and conditions of life and death.
In this region as well, there are those who worship the deity of the skull to speak of the world’s prosperity or decline.
Divination by means of milfoil stalks or tortoise shells is for resolving doubts.

Both of these are heterodox arts that delude the human mind; having been practiced as a habit through successive generations, they benefit neither oneself nor others, and are therefore prohibited and penalized.
As for those who serve as messengers for thieves, they are employed by bandits to assist in the commission of theft.
From the perspective of contributing conditions, it is classified as a light offense;
however, if the act constitutes the karma of theft, it logically falls under the category of grave offenses.
Third, regarding the commission of an offense due to violating regulations, it is as stated in the text.
Thirty-fourth, one should maintain mindfulness of the precepts of the Hīnayāna.
The Bodhisattva’s mind consists of the four great vows without interruption;
because mixing right and wrong makes the Great Way difficult to attain, these transgressions are thus proscribed.
There are three distinct conditions:
first, a lack of diligent protection;
second, the mental preoccupation with a minor school.
Third, regarding the abandonment of the great and the indulgence in the small, one commits an offense in a single thought-moment.
This section consists of two parts:
first, the designation of the name and the establishment of the precept.
Next, if one gives rise to an inferior state that violates the regulations, an offense is incurred.
Regarding the initial statement "guarding and maintaining" (*ārakṣaṇa-saṃvara*): "guarding" (*ārakṣaṇa*) means protecting; "maintaining" (*saṃvara*) means holding through mindfulness.
There are two kinds of maintenance: because it stops evil, the essence of the precepts remains unimpaired, which is called "maintenance by stopping" (*vāraṇa-saṃvara*).
To cultivate in accordance with the teachings so that the precepts become radiant and pure is called "active observance" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*).
Both types of observance are termed "precepts" (*śīla*) because they are accomplished through protection.
Therefore, when the three karmas function in unison, it is called "protective observance of the prohibitions" (*saṃvara-śīla*).
Therefore, by regulating the four modes of deportment, one restrains body and mind;
by reciting and chanting during the six periods of the day, one disciplines the mouth.
Through the external support of the Dharma-rain, the conditions of the mind accord with the principle of nature.
Because it is firm and difficult to move, it is likened to a vajra.
The various meditative concentrations (samādhi) are like a life-preserving float.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
It is, for example, like a person who, carrying a life-preserving float, wishes to cross the great ocean.
At that time, a rākṣasa from within the sea comes to beg for the float;
at first he begs for it whole, and even when asked for as little as a speck of dust, [the person] gives nothing at all.
This illustrates the characteristics of the various meditative concentrations (samādhi).
The two types of death—segmented and transformative—are as deep and vast as the great ocean;
the realization of the fruit of the three virtues is like reaching the further shore.
The life-preserving bag of precepts must remain free of leaks so that the further shore may be reached;
yet if it is damaged even by a needle’s eye, the waters of craving and false views will gradually enter the body and mind,
leading from small faults to great calamities.
In the saṃsāra of the six realms, one loses the name of wisdom and dies submerged in the ocean of existence.
The case of the "grass-tied bhikṣu" illustrates this aforementioned meaning:
to protect against even minor transgressions, one should not violate them even at the cost of one's life.
In the *Vyavahāra-śāstra*, it is recorded that when some thieves who had stolen the king’s property encountered a bhikṣu, they feared their deed would be exposed.
They consulted among themselves, saying, "I have heard that bhikṣus do not damage living grass; let us lead [the victim] to the side of the road and bind him with grass."
The king went out on a hunting excursion and spoke this verse, asking:
"I observe that this bhikṣu is stout and possesses great strength; by what cause and condition is he bound by grass and unable to turn over?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"When I observed this grass, it was extremely fragile;
I feared that if I were to turn over, I would violate the Tathāgata’s prohibition."
The king then released him and made a vow to protect the Dharma;
that he never let this thought depart from his mind is what is meant by "renunciation" (śe).
The mind and its continuum do not abandon [the practice] for even a single moment;
because one takes the Three Jewels as the singular object and gives rise to the Four Great Vows, it is said that "one is constantly born [in them]," and so forth.
Next, regarding the summary of transgressions, the mention of "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika) implies that the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are themselves non-Buddhists.
Because they are outside the Perfect Way, they are called "external paths" (tīrthika).
The thirty-five precepts on not making the ten vows are for the Bodhisattva to make vows so that the mind does not regress and practice has a definitive destination.
Therefore, one does not commit an offense without having made a vow;
specifically, two conditions must be met:
first, the failure to make a vow.
Second, regarding the offenses committed through negligence and forgetfulness after having undertaken the precepts, there are three sections according to the text.
First, the names are designated and the general number is enumerated; thus it says "all."
Next, following "filial piety and obedience," the ten vows are listed individually.
Third, from "if all" onwards, the violation of the regulations and the resulting offense are concluded according to the text.
Within the subsequent individual listing, filial piety and obedience toward parents, teachers, and the Sangha constitute two [vows].
Third, may I obtain good teachers and friends.
Fourth, may they constantly teach me the Mahāyāna.
Fifth, may they constantly teach me the Ten Abodes.
Sixth, may you always teach me the Ten Dedications.
Eighth, may you always teach me the Ten Stages.
Ninth, may you cause me to attain understanding and practice in accordance with the Dharma.
The tenth vow is to firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts.
Since the firm upholding of the Buddha’s precepts applies to both the beginning and the end,
we know that the ten vows are complete with respect to both cause and effect.
The "Sublime Enlightenment" (Miaojue) is not listed here in brief because it represents the ultimate goal of practice and the finality of realization.

Since the causes and fruits of one's own practice, as well as self-benefit and benefit for others, are fully contained herein, it inherently encompasses the agent and object of the capacity to transform others.
In the practice of cultivation through awakening and understanding, what dharma is not fully contained?
All the dharmas for transforming beings throughout a single lifetime are subsumed therein.
Therefore, one is cautioned and exhorted never to abandon this for even a moment; thus it is said that "thought after thought, it does not depart."
The rules for the formation of offenses are as stated in the text.
